anchor.quote: only an equal-or-stronger judge may vouch

body: In this plan, if the judge is equal and is not a frontier model, then a warning in the harness should point this out.  For example, if Qwen is both task runner and judge, we should get a warning, but if Opus is both task runner and judge then no warning should appear.  I'm not sure if you'll be able to detect this.  Maybe we can only detect in the model provider whether it is using local inference vs. cloud inference?
So for example, a task model runner in the end, may be using Opus (because of graduation), but the judge may be Sonnet 5.  Should we consider auto-elevating the judge in this case?

anchor.quote: surface a judge weaker than the actor it verifies

body: Is this surfaced on harness startup or JIT.  Since a task runner can graduate with re-attempts, it matters.  Right?

Accepted, and your fallback guess became the rule. The equal-but-weak case is called out in 'The principle' and drives Decision 2's bump. Detection is Decision 7: the 'strength' rank when declared, and exactly your suggestion - provider kind (local vs cloud) - whenever strength is 'unspecified'. So it works on a registry you never annotate, and sharpens when you do. One correction the DoR pass surfaced: provider kind alone can't decide it in general, because 'openai-compat' covers BOTH a loopback Ollama endpoint and a cloud OpenAI-compatible API. So the kind-fallback is scoped to the VERIFIER side only (where a wrong guess costs one spare advisory) and forbidden for actor ordering (where it would misroute real spend). You ratified that fix.

Yes - Decision 6 re-resolves the judge upward on every escalation. But the naive answer is now wrong, and this is the sharpest interaction in the plan: your own bump-ceiling answer forbids the harness from auto-selecting a costly model. If Opus carries costly:true, the judge CANNOT be auto-elevated to meet it. The rule degrades rather than overspends - it emits the #229 advisory and the run proceeds. You confirmed this ('costly is never automatic'), including the sharp edge: marking your only hard-capable block costly makes the 'hard' tier unservable, as a validate-time GR2046 error rather than something to route around. DoR section 14.1 shows the exact error text a user meets.

Right, and it settled the check-timing question as BOTH (Decision 9). Your reasoning is exactly why startup alone is insufficient - a tier reached by graduating mid-run is invisible to any preflight - while the preflight still earns its place by catching a misconfigured plan before a token is spent. Note the DoR revision initially tried to defer the JIT half to v2 on the grounds that static v1 has no graduation to observe; you overruled that and it is now v1 in full. The strongest argument for it turned out not to be graduation at all: the preflight is a MODEL of the resolver, the JIT check IS the resolver, and any disagreement between them is a resolver bug no preflight could catch.
